anomaly_def.Name: Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : Sustained reads or writes saturate the physical storage subsystem, driving up latency, queue depth, and I/O-related wait events.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : Kernel-enforced ceilings on file handles, shared memory, threads, or other per-process quotas prevent the database from allocating required operating-system objects.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Transport, listener, socket, or authentication resources between clients and the server are exhausted or slowed, impeding connection establishment and data transfer.

When all three root causes occur concurrently, the database exhibits a multi-layer resource gridlock: I/O wait times surge while sessions already connected cannot read from or write to disk promptly; at the same time, new or parallel sessions may fail to spawn because the kernel refuses additional threads, file descriptors, or AIO contexts, and clients attempting to connect face timeouts or refusals as listener backlogs and socket queues overflow. Observable metrics become noisy and intertwined—CPU appears idle, yet transaction latency climbs; wait profiles show a mixture of storage waits, client I/O waits, and internal latch or semaphore allocation failures; system logs alternate between kernel "out of resources" messages and network stack "connection reset" or "cannot allocate socket" errors. Batch windows stretch, OLTP response times spike, and connection-pool retry storms amplify both network and storage pressure, making it difficult to attribute symptoms to a single layer.

Causally, saturated storage bandwidth forces background writers and log flushers to hold file descriptors and AIO contexts for longer periods, rapidly consuming the limited kernel resources governed by per-process limits. As these limits are reached, new I/O contexts and threads cannot be created, causing further backlog in the I/O submission path and lengthening storage queues. Simultaneously, exhausted file handles and listener socket quotas prevent timely acceptance of new TCP connections, which causes clients to retry aggressively, inflating the connection rate and deepening the socket backlog. The compounded effect is a feedback loop in which storage stalls increase kernel resource retention, depleted kernel resources hinder both I/O and connection handling, and network retries multiply the load, jointly degrading overall database availability and performance far more severely than any single anomaly would alone.

entry.official_description: Got a read error from the connection pipe
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with connection establishment, authentication exchange, protocol correctness, network reachability, or client/server communication stability.
entry.solution_guidance: Check endpoint reachability, authentication flow, connection limits, protocol compatibility, transport stability, and client connection lifecycle management.
